title: Raoul Nijhorst - Studio Art-Nude Photography Instructional (Dutch, clickbait-retitled)
summary: A Dutch instructional DVD by photographer Raoul Nijhorst on studio art-nude work, retitled with English clickbait on YouTube; the actual content is a straight technical and professional-conduct course. Roughly half is set ethics and business practice - sourcing models, chaperones, on-set conduct rules, and a written model release - and half is hard studio craft: light-modifier hardness, striplights and rim light, beauty dish, white/black/grey/silhouette background control by metering, viewpoint and focal-length distortion, props, macro abstraction, makeup as in-camera dodge-and-burn, and a short Photoshop pass. Its core lighting principle is the same physics as the harsh-daylight material: hardness is set by the SIZE OF THE SOURCE RELATIVE TO THE SUBJECT, which is why the sun - enormous but distant - behaves as a point source and throws hard midday shadows.

steps.action: Sourcing models: re-book someone you have already shot, approach via model platforms or social, and offer that they bring a parent or partner along. Build a portfolio FIRST so the approach reads as serious work; workshops break the chicken-and-egg of needing nude work to get nude work.

On-set conduct rules, stated as non-negotiable: never leave the model unnecessarily undressed or waiting; turn away while they adjust hair or pose and do not stare; no sexist remarks; never touch the model; never make advances; no alcohol on set - use social skills to relax someone, not drink.

Have lights positioned, light metered and camera configured BEFORE the model undresses - fumbling settings while someone waits undressed is the failure mode. Dry-run the setup fully clothed, confirm pose and lighting, then ask them to undress and reshoot.

Work from a written contract. His release: model may use the images for her portfolio with photographer credit; photographer may use them for his portfolio; NEITHER party may sell them commercially - personal use only.
Hard vs soft light demonstrated. Bare reflector = hard, read it off the sharp-edged cast shadow behind and on the subject. Softbox = soft, shadow nearly absent.

THE governing principle: hardness is the size of the source RELATIVE TO THE SUBJECT. Moving the same softbox far away makes it small relative to the model and hard again. The sun is the limiting case - vast, but so distant it is effectively a point, hence hard midday shadows.

Striplight (1.80m, long and narrow): lights the full body top-to-bottom where a small softbox only covers the upper half. Placed behind the subject it gives rim light, separating the model from the background.
Hardness ladder for accents: reflector < reflector+grid < snoot < snoot+grid. The hardest are not aimed straight at the model - use them as hair light or to accent a specific area.

Beauty dish at ~45 degrees above, square-on: symmetric lighting that accentuates the jawline, and a ROUND catchlight where a softbox leaves a rectangle. Fill the resulting hard under-chin shadow with a reflector board; flip to the softer side of the board to taper the fill.

Continuous light vs flash is preference only - he takes continuous for what-you-see-is-what-you-get and no surprises. Every technique shown transfers to strobes unchanged; do not go buy continuous lights on account of it.
Vary the viewpoint. From a ladder for a high angle; from the floor for a low angle, which lengthens the legs but COMPRESSES the torso - real distortion, so confirm the model is comfortable with it.

Focal-length comparison at fixed framing: 16mm (heavy distortion) -> 24mm -> 70mm -> 200mm. The long end gives the most flattering rendering of the body; where you stand and what lens you pick IS the photograph.

White background control by metering: hold about 2 stops between background and subject - background metered f/11.5, subject f/5.6-6.5. Same white paper then yields GREY by killing the background lights, and a SILHOUETTE by killing the front light and keeping the back lights.

Black background for low-key mood work. Props earn their place twice: boxing gloves add visual interest AND make the model feel less exposed. A plant sprayer puts water droplets on skin for a dimensional 3D effect; chocolate sauce for abstract work, applied sparingly - less is more.

Abstract body-form work on a 100mm macro at ISO 400, 1/250, f/2.8 - shallow focus for defamiliarized shapes. Shutter kept at 1/250 rather than 1/100 as insurance for handheld work at that focal length. Lens hoods used INDOORS too, to stop studio light causing internal reflection.

Makeup artist segment: 'shaping' the body with light and dark makeup is dodge-and-burn done in camera - lighter advances, darker recedes - and saves the retouching pass. Always ask the model what THEY want addressed. Kit: foundation/blush/powder brushes, DISPOSABLE sponges for hygiene when working on the body, and concealers and foundations across multiple skin tones.

Post pass: clone tool (alt-click to set source, resample often) to remove an intruding ceiling; black solid-color adjustment layer set to blend mode COLOR for black-and-white; spot healing brush for temporary marks; crop to strengthen the frame. Ethic stated: remove TEMPORARY blemishes, keep permanent features - the piercing and tattoo stay.
steps.code: Solid Color layer (black) -> blend mode: Color

key_takeaways: Light hardness is governed by source size RELATIVE to subject - the same softbox pulled back becomes a hard source, which is exactly why the sun reads as a point and throws hard midday shadows.

Consent and conduct are procedure, not sentiment: no unnecessary exposure time, look away during adjustments, no touching, no advances, no alcohol on set, and a written release covering portfolio use both ways with no commercial sale by either party.
Meter and configure everything with the model still clothed; dry-run the pose, confirm the light, and only then ask them to undress.
One white background yields three looks purely by metering and switching lights: white at ~2 stops over the subject, grey with the back lights off, silhouette with the front light off.
Striplights cover a full standing body where a small softbox only covers the top half, and double as rim light from behind.
Beauty dish gives round catchlights and jawline definition; a softbox leaves rectangles. Fill the under-chin shadow with a board.
Low camera angles lengthen legs but compress the torso, and long lenses flatter the body while wide lenses distort it - position and focal length are compositional decisions, not conveniences.
Makeup 'shaping' is dodge-and-burn performed before the shutter, and it is cheaper than doing it in post.
Master one light before adding a second; grow with the gear rather than buying a battery of it up front.
